prompt:
Tamsin is developing a rostering app for Wombat Gully Community Radio in Daylesford. The station manager commissioned the app, but it will be used by the volunteer presenters, most of whom are retirees who use their phones to claim and swap shifts.

Describe how Tamsin could apply user-centred design while she develops the app.

points.text: Involves representative users, the volunteer presenters (not only the station manager), in trying mock-ups or early versions of the app
Gathers their feedback on real tasks, such as claiming or swapping a shift, for example by observing them or asking them
Revises the design in response to the feedback and has the volunteers try the revised version again

model: Tamsin should involve the people who will actually use the app: the volunteer presenters, many of them retirees using phones, not only the station manager. She could give a small group an early version and watch them claim and swap shifts, noting where they hesitate or make mistakes, and ask what they found difficult. She would then change the design in response, for example by enlarging buttons or reducing the steps needed to swap a shift, and have the volunteers try the revised version, repeating this until the app suits them.
mistake: Saying that user-centred design meets users' needs earns nothing on its own. Describe how the actual users, named from the scenario, are involved at each stage and how their feedback changes the design.

prompt:
Silky Oak Physio in Ballarat has made two changes to its appointment program:

1. Receptionists now pick the appointment date from a calendar control instead of typing it.
2. Before an appointment is saved, the program checks that the physiotherapist isn't already booked at that time.

For each change, explain how it improves the efficiency or the effectiveness of the program.

points.text: Change 1: identifies an improvement in efficiency (or in effectiveness, when justified by fewer incorrectly entered dates)
Change 1: explains that picking a date needs fewer keystrokes and less effort than typing it (or that it prevents badly formatted or impossible dates)
Change 2: identifies an improvement in effectiveness
Change 2: explains that it prevents double bookings, so the appointment records are accurate and no patient is booked into a time that is already taken

model:
Change 1 improves efficiency. Picking a date from a calendar control replaces typing it in full, so each booking needs fewer keystrokes and less effort from the receptionist.

Change 2 improves effectiveness. Checking for an existing appointment before saving prevents two patients being booked with the same physiotherapist at the same time, so the appointment records are accurate and the program better achieves its purpose of scheduling patients correctly.
mistake: Blurring the two qualities loses marks: efficiency is the time, cost and effort used, while effectiveness is how well the program achieves its purpose, such as keeping accurate records. Name the quality each change improves and give a separate reason for each.

prompt:
Lina is developing a check-in app for the Cherry Ballart Farmers' Market in Alexandra. On market mornings, volunteers at the gate will use the app on a shared tablet to record each stallholder's arrival, confirm their site number and record that their stall fee has been paid, often while a queue of vans waits to get in. Most volunteers work at the gate only once a month. The market's coordinator has described what she wants, but Lina plans to spend the first week of the eight-week project watching volunteers check stallholders in with the current paper list, and having them try paper mock-ups of her screens. The coordinator thinks this wastes a week.

Justify Lina's plan.

points.text: Watching volunteers at the gate shows how check-in really happens, e.g. a queue of vans waiting, or volunteers who work there only once a month and won't remember complicated steps, which the coordinator's description may leave out, so the app can be designed for these conditions
Problems found with paper mock-ups can be fixed quickly before any code is written, saving the time it would take to rewrite and retest code later in the eight weeks
An app designed around how the volunteers actually work is more likely to be used correctly, so check-in records are more accurate and complete and the app is more effective

model:
The coordinator's description is second-hand. Watching volunteers check stallholders in shows how it really happens: at the gate, with a queue of vans waiting, and by volunteers who work there only once a month and so can't be expected to remember complicated steps. Lina can design for these conditions, for example with few steps on each screen, only once she has seen them.

Having volunteers try paper mock-ups finds confusing screens before any code exists. Changing a drawing takes minutes, while changing finished code means rewriting and retesting it, so the week is likely to save time later in the eight-week project.

Finally, an app built around how the volunteers actually work is more likely to be used correctly, so each stallholder's arrival, site and fee are recorded accurately and completely, and the app is more effective at its purpose.
mistake: Justify needs reasons tied to the scenario. Saying that user-centred design is good practice earns little; say what watching these volunteers would reveal, and why that matters for this app.

prompt:
Bettong Community Transport, a volunteer service in Benalla, drives older residents to medical appointments. At present, the booking coordinator writes each request in a paper diary and phones around the volunteer drivers to arrange it. A new app will replace the diary: residents will request rides on their phones, the coordinator will assign each ride to a driver, and drivers will see their pick-ups on a tablet in the car. Hamish, the developer, plans to use user-centred design.

Explain how Hamish's use of user-centred design would help make the app both efficient and effective.

points.text: Explains that the actual users (residents, the booking coordinator and the volunteer drivers) are involved at every stage, for example interviewed during analysis, trying mock-ups during design and beta testing a near-finished version, so feedback is gathered early and the design is revised in response

Gives an efficiency example tied to the scenario that saves time, cost or effort and follows from involving users, e.g. watching the coordinator match rides to drivers leads to a screen that lists the drivers free for each ride, so a ride is assigned in a few taps instead of by phoning around, or drivers see changed pick-ups on the tablet without calling the office

Gives an effectiveness example tied to the scenario, e.g. booking screens tested by residents lead to fewer wrong dates or pick-up addresses, so fewer rides are missed, or residents get clear confirmation that a ride is booked

model:
User-centred design means the people who will actually use the app take part at every stage of its development. Hamish could interview residents, the booking coordinator and drivers during analysis, have each group try mock-ups of their screens during design, and beta test a near-finished version with them on their own phones and the car tablets. Their feedback arrives early, while changes are quick to make, and he revises the design in response.

This makes the app more efficient. By watching the coordinator arrange rides now, Hamish sees that arranging each ride starts with finding which drivers are free at the pick-up time. He can then design a screen that lists the free drivers for each request, so a ride can be assigned in a few taps instead of phoning around, saving time and effort on every booking.

It also makes the app more effective. Residents who try the booking screens can show Hamish where they enter the wrong date or pick-up address, so the final screens lead to fewer booking errors and missed rides, and each resident gets a clear confirmation that their ride is booked.
mistake: Saying only that user-centred design 'meets the users' needs', without describing how users take part, earned no marks in 2025. Show how the users named in the scenario take part at each stage, then give a separate efficiency example (time, cost or effort saved) and effectiveness example (fewer errors, clearer feedback).

prompt:
Coralie is developing a stock program for Mountain Ash Hollow Nursery in Emerald. When the program starts, it reads `stock.csv`, where each line holds a plant code (e.g. LR-0193), plant name, quantity on hand and price (e.g. 14.95). Staff search for and update plants during the day, and the program writes the stock list back to the file when it closes.

Justify a data structure for holding the stock list while the program runs, and a data type for each of the quantity on hand and the price.

points.text: Identifies an array of records, with one record per plant
Justifies it: each record keeps one plant's fields, of different data types, together under names, and the array lets the program loop through or search all plants
Quantity on hand as integer, because it is a whole number of plants that is added to and subtracted from
Price as floating point, to two decimal places, because it is in dollars and cents and is used in calculations

model:
An array of records suits the stock list. Each record holds one plant's code, name, quantity and price together, even though these have different data types, and each field can be referred to by name. Holding one record per plant in an array lets the program loop through every plant to find or update one.

Quantity on hand should be an integer, because the nursery counts whole plants and the quantity is added to and subtracted from as stock arrives and sells. Price should be floating point, to two decimal places, because prices such as $14.95 are in dollars and cents and are used in calculations, such as the value of stock.
mistake: Shortened type names such as Float or Bool earned no marks in 2025, so write them in full: integer, floating point. Tie each justification to the data in the scenario rather than giving a general definition.

prompt:
Alpine Ash Ski Hire in Mansfield exports each day's hires from its booking system to `hires.csv`. Each line holds a customer name, the number of days hired and the daily rate, for example:

`Dimitri Pappas,3,42.50`

Omar's reporting program reads the file and calculates the day's total hire income. Explain **three** things the program must do with each line so that the hire's income is added to the total.

points.text: Splits the line at each comma to separate the name, the number of days and the daily rate
Converts the days to integer and the rate to floating point, because the fields split from the line are strings
Multiplies the days by the daily rate and adds the result to the running total
Alternative: checks that each field is present and numeric before converting, so a damaged line doesn't cause a runtime error

model: First, the program splits the line at each comma, separating the name (Dimitri Pappas), the days (3) and the rate (42.50) into three fields. Second, because the fields split from a line of text are strings, it converts the days to an integer and the rate to floating point; without this, "3" and "42.50" can't be multiplied. Third, it multiplies the days by the rate (3 × 42.50 = 127.50) and adds the result to the running total for the day.
mistake: The conversion step is the one most often left out. Fields split from a line of text stay strings until the program converts them.

prompt:
Jasmine is developing a program for Rosella Spur Walking Club in Bright to manage its walk leaders. For each leader, the program must remember their name, their leader grade (1, 2 or 3) and whether they hold a current first aid certificate, and it must keep this list between runs. Once a month, the club secretary opens the list in a spreadsheet to check which certificates have lapsed.

Recommend how the program should store the list of leaders between runs, and explain how the program should handle the list when it starts and when it closes.

points.text: Recommends a CSV file, with one leader per line and the fields separated by commas
Justifies it: every leader has the same three fields, and the secretary's spreadsheet can open a CSV file directly, putting each field in its own column

When the program starts: reads the file line by line, splits each line at the commas, converts the grade to integer and the certificate field to Boolean, and stores each leader as a record in an array
When the program closes (or after each change): writes every record in the array back to the file, one line per leader, so that changes made while it ran aren't lost

model:
The list should be stored in a CSV file, with one leader per line and the name, grade and certificate fields separated by commas, for example `Mara Quinlan,2,True`. Every leader has the same three fields, so a flat file suits the data, and the secretary can open a CSV file directly in a spreadsheet, with each field in its own column, to check certificates each month.

When the program starts, it reads the file line by line. It splits each line at the commas, converts the grade to an integer and the certificate field to a Boolean, since each field is read from the file as text, and stores each leader as a record in an array. When the program closes, or straight after each change, it writes every record back to the file, one line per leader. Data held in the array is lost when the program closes, so without this step any new leaders or updated certificates would be lost.
mistake: Data held in an array isn't kept between runs. The program must write the list back to the file, or every change made since it started is lost.

prompt:
Nadia is developing an online booking form for Kookaburra Creek Kayak Tours in Mallacoota. Her first version uses a text box for every input. The form collects:

- the tour (one of four tours)
- the number of paddlers (1 to 8)
- whether the customer wants to hire a wetsuit
- the customer's name

Recommend a more suitable GUI control for the tour, the number of paddlers and the wetsuit hire, and explain how using these controls improves the accuracy of bookings.

points.text: Tour: radio buttons or a drop-down list, because exactly one of four fixed tours is chosen
Number of paddlers: a drop-down list (or number spinner) limited to 1 to 8
Wetsuit hire: a check box, because the answer is yes or no
Explains that the controls allow only valid values, so misspelt tours and non-numeric or out-of-range numbers can't be entered

model:
The tour should use radio buttons (or a drop-down list), so the customer picks one of the four tours instead of typing a name that could be misspelt. The number of paddlers should use a drop-down list, or a number spinner, that offers only 1 to 8. Wetsuit hire should use a check box, since the answer is simply yes or no.

These controls offer only valid values, so a customer can't enter a tour that doesn't exist, text such as "four" for the number of paddlers, or a group of 12. Bookings are more accurate, and the program needs fewer type and range checks on these fields, although it should still check that a tour has been chosen.

prompt:
Bluetongue Miniature Railway in Castlemaine charges by age: children under 4 ride free, riders aged 4 to 15 pay $6, and riders aged 16 and over pay $10.

Write pseudocode for a function `ticketPrice` that takes a rider's age as a parameter and returns the price.

points.text: A function header naming `ticketPrice` with a parameter for the age, closed with ENDFUNCTION
Selection with correct boundaries: under 4 gives 0, 4 to 15 gives 6, and 16 and over gives 10
Returns the price to the caller with RETURN, rather than displaying it

model:
```pseudo
FUNCTION ticketPrice(age)
    IF age < 4 THEN
        price ← 0
    ELSEIF age <= 15 THEN
        price ← 6
    ELSE
        price ← 10
    ENDIF
    RETURN price
ENDFUNCTION
```

Ages 3, 4, 15 and 16 return 0, 6, 6 and 10, which checks each boundary.
mistake: Check each boundary. Writing `age < 15` instead of `age <= 15` would charge a 15-year-old $10.

prompt:
Jonas is developing a membership program for Rufous Whistler Birdwatchers, a club in Wodonga. When the program starts, it opens `members.csv` and reads each member into an array of records; when it closes, it writes the array back to the file. Jonas tested the program on his own computer, where `members.csv` already existed. When the club secretary first ran it on her new laptop, where the file hadn't been created yet, the program stopped with an error as soon as it started.

Explain why the program stopped, and describe how Jonas should change the program so that it handles this situation.

points.text: Explains that the program tries to open `members.csv` for reading, but the file doesn't exist on the new laptop, so opening it fails while the program runs (a runtime error), and nothing in the program handles that case
Describes checking whether the file exists before opening it (or handling the error that opening it raises), instead of assuming the file is there
Describes what the program does when the file is missing: it starts with an empty array of members instead of reading, and the file is created when the program first writes the members to it
Alternative: displays a message telling the secretary that no member file was found and a new one will be created, so a file that has been moved or renamed by mistake is noticed

model:
The program assumes that `members.csv` exists. On Jonas's computer it did, so his tests passed, but on the secretary's new laptop the file hadn't been created yet. When the program tried to open it for reading, the open operation failed while the program was running, a runtime error, and because nothing in the program handles that case, the program stopped.

Jonas should make the program check whether `members.csv` exists before opening it, or handle the error that opening it raises. If the file exists, the program reads the members as before. If it doesn't, the program starts with an empty array of members instead of reading, and the file is created the first time the program writes the members to it, when it closes. The program could also display a message such as "No member file found; a new one will be created", so that the secretary would notice if the file had been moved or renamed by mistake.
mistake: 'Add error handling' on its own earns little. Say what the program checks before it opens the file, and what it does when the file is missing.

prompt:
Fergus is developing the check-in program for Feathertail Bouldering, a climbing gym in Stawell. Climbers buy a pass that holds a number of visits. The `VisitPass` class is described below, with no access modifiers yet. Fergus's notes on the class say:

- No code outside `VisitPass` may change `visitsLeft`. It changes only when the front-desk screen records a visit or sells extra visits.
- The front-desk screen displays the holder's name and the visits left, and staff can correct a misspelt name.
- `passID` and `expiryDate` are used only by the methods of `VisitPass`.
- `isExpired()` is called only by `recordVisit()`.
- A subclass, `SchoolPass (extends VisitPass)`, has a method that works out a school group's price, and it must use `pricePerVisit` directly. No other class may use `pricePerVisit`.

Complete the object description by writing an access modifier (public, protected or private) before each property and each method. Justify your choices for `visitsLeft`, `isExpired()` and `pricePerVisit`.

points.text: Writes private before `passID`, `holderName`, `visitsLeft` and `expiryDate`.
Writes public before `getHolderName()`, `setHolderName(name)`, `getVisitsLeft()`, `recordVisit()` and `buyVisits(extraVisits)`, because the front-desk screen calls them.

Justifies private for `visitsLeft`: only the methods of `VisitPass` can change it, so other code can't, for example, add visits without a sale; every change goes through `recordVisit()` or `buyVisits(extraVisits)`, which can check it first. (Protected would also let the methods of `SchoolPass` change it.)

Justifies private for `isExpired()`: it is called only by `recordVisit()`, a method of the same class, so no other class needs it, and hiding it keeps the class's public methods to those other code uses.

Justifies protected for `pricePerVisit`: the methods of the subclass `SchoolPass` can use it directly while unrelated classes can't; private would block `SchoolPass`, and public would let any class read or change it.

model:
**Name:** VisitPass

**Properties/Attributes:**

- `private passID (string)`
- `private holderName (string)`
- `private visitsLeft (integer)`
- `private expiryDate (date/time)`
- `protected pricePerVisit (floating point)`

**Methods:**

- `public getHolderName()`
- `public setHolderName(name)`
- `public getVisitsLeft()`
- `public recordVisit()`
- `public buyVisits(extraVisits)`
- `private isExpired()`

`visitsLeft` is private, so only the methods of `VisitPass` can change it. The front-desk screen can't set it directly, for example to add visits without a sale. It must call `recordVisit()` or `buyVisits(extraVisits)`, which can check each change before it is stored, and it reads the value through `getVisitsLeft()`. Protected wouldn't meet Fergus's note, because the methods of `SchoolPass` could then change it.

`isExpired()` is private because only `recordVisit()`, inside the same class, calls it. No other class needs it, so hiding it keeps the public methods to those the front-desk screen uses, and Fergus can change it later without affecting other classes.

`pricePerVisit` is protected because the method in the `SchoolPass` subclass must use it directly. Protected lets `VisitPass` and its subclasses use it while hiding it from unrelated classes. Private would stop `SchoolPass` using it, and public would let any class read or change the price.
mistake: Protected doesn't keep a member inside its own class: subclasses can use it too. On the 2025 exam, a fifth of students chose protected for an attribute that only its own class's methods could use, which needs private.

prompt:
Ellie is developing a booking app for Brolga Wetlands Tours in Kerang. The app uses a third-party weather API to warn customers when strong winds may cancel a boat tour.

Explain one risk of relying on this API, and describe two ways Ellie could reduce the impact of that risk.

points.text: Explains a risk and its effect on the app, e.g. the provider changes its data format, starts charging or revokes access, so wind warnings stop working
One way to reduce the impact, e.g. keeping all calls to the API in one module, so only that module needs changing
A second way, e.g. a fallback such as showing the last saved forecast or switching to another provider, or monitoring the provider's notices of changes

model:
The weather API is controlled by its provider, not by Ellie. If the provider changes the format of its data, starts charging, or revokes the app's access, the app's requests will fail and customers won't be warned about winds that may cancel their tour.

Ellie could keep every call to the weather API in a single module, so that if the API changes, only that module needs to be rewritten and retested. She could also build a fallback: if a request fails, the app shows the most recent forecast it saved, with the time it was issued, or requests the forecast from a second provider, so customers still receive a warning.

prompt:
Three developers at Redthroat Software in Wodonga are building a booking system for a local council. At present they email copies of their code files to each other, and last week one developer's changes overwrote another's.

Describe **two** benefits of storing the team's code in a shared code repository.

points.text: Benefit 1: every change is recorded with who made it and when, giving a history of the code
Applies benefit 1: e.g. the team can find which change introduced an error and roll back to the last working version
Benefit 2: all developers work from one shared copy, and their changes are merged into it instead of one copy replacing another
Applies benefit 2: e.g. last week's lost work wouldn't happen, because both developers' changes are kept and any conflicting lines are flagged for them to resolve

model:
First, the repository records every change with its author, the date and a message. If the booking system starts producing errors, the team can see exactly what changed since the last working version and roll back that change, instead of guessing which emailed file is current.

Second, all three developers work from one shared copy of the code. When two of them change the same file, the version control tool merges their changes and flags any lines that conflict for them to resolve, so one developer's work can't silently overwrite another's, as happened last week.

prompt:
Mei is the only developer building a stock app for Messmate Hardware, which has three stores in South Gippsland. Staff will scan product barcodes with the camera on a store tablet. Mei estimates that writing her own barcode-reading module would take four weeks of her ten-week schedule. She has found an open-source barcode library that is used by thousands of developers and updated regularly. Its licence allows use in commercial software, provided its authors are acknowledged.

Recommend whether Mei should use the library or write her own module, and justify your recommendation.

points.text: Recommends using the library
Justifies with time: it saves about four of the ten weeks, leaving time for the app's other modules and for testing
Justifies with quality: a library used by thousands of developers and updated regularly is likely to be better tested and more reliable than a module written quickly by one developer
Addresses a condition or risk, e.g. acknowledging the library's authors as the licence requires, or keeping to a tested version of the library and re-testing the app before upgrading

model:
Mei should use the library. Writing her own barcode module would take four of her ten weeks, leaving little time for the app's other modules and for testing; the library lets her spend that time on the parts only she can build.

The library is also likely to be more reliable than her own module. Thousands of developers use it and it is updated regularly, so errors are more likely to have been found and fixed than in code she writes under time pressure.

She must meet the licence's condition by acknowledging the library's authors, for example in the app's documentation. To manage the risk of a future version changing how it works, she should keep using the version she has tested, and re-test the app before upgrading.
mistake: Using a library doesn't remove the developer's responsibilities. Its licence conditions must be met, and each new version must be tested before the program uses it.

prompt:
Rhiannon works for Kangaroo Grass Beef, a cattle producer near Hamilton. She has been asked to write code that calculates each steer's average daily weight gain from its weigh-in records. Each record holds the date of the weigh-in and the steer's weight in kilograms, and a missed weigh-in is recorded with a weight of 0. Rhiannon has never calculated weight gain before, so she asks an AI-based assistant to generate the code, typing only *average daily weight gain for cattle*.

Explain **two** reasons why the code the assistant generates may not be reliable.

points.text: Outlines a first reason. For example: the assistant lacks context, because it knows only Rhiannon's short prompt and not how the producer's weigh-in records are stored.

Relates the first reason to Rhiannon's task. For example: the assistant doesn't know that 0 means a missed weigh-in, so the code may treat 0 as a real weight and show a steer that missed its latest weigh-in as losing hundreds of kilograms; or it may assume a different unit or record layout.

Outlines a second, different reason. For example: generated code can look correct and run without errors but still contain logic errors or miss cases (lack of accuracy); or it may call a function that doesn't exist in the language Rhiannon uses.

Relates the second reason to Rhiannon's task. For example: the code might divide the gain by the number of weigh-ins instead of the number of days between the first and last weigh-in, or fail for a steer with only one weigh-in; because Rhiannon has never done this calculation, she may not notice unless she checks the results against gains worked out by hand.

model:
First, the assistant lacks context about Rhiannon's data. Her prompt didn't say that each record holds a date and a weight in kilograms, or that a weight of 0 means the steer missed a weigh-in. The generated code may therefore treat 0 as a real weight, so a steer that missed its latest weigh-in would appear to have lost hundreds of kilograms, and its average daily gain would be badly wrong even though the code runs.

Second, the generated code may be inaccurate even if it looks correct and runs without errors. It could, for example, divide the total gain by the number of weigh-ins rather than by the number of days between the first and last weigh-in, or fail for a steer with only one weigh-in. Because Rhiannon has never calculated weight gain, she may not be able to spot these errors by reading the code, so wrong figures could be reported unless she tests the code against gains she has worked out by hand.
mistake: A reason that fits any program, such as 'AI can make mistakes', earns little. Say what the assistant didn't know or could get wrong in this task and what wrong result that would give. Reliability is about whether the code gives correct results, not about privacy or whether using AI is allowed.

prompt:
Brushtail Bike Hire in Beechworth has a hire program. Staff type the length of each hire, in whole hours from 1 to 8, into a text box. At present the program crashes if a staff member types letters, and it accepts hires of 0 and 40 hours.

Describe the validation the program needs for the hire length, including the order of the checks and what the program should do when a check fails.

points.text: Existence check: the hire length hasn't been left blank
Type check: the entry is a whole number, applied before it is converted to integer, which prevents the crash when letters are typed
Range check: the hire length is from 1 to 8 inclusive, which rejects 0 and 40
When a check fails: displays a message stating what is accepted and asks again, without processing the hire

model:
The program first applies an existence check, rejecting the entry if the hire length is blank. Next it applies a type check, confirming that the entry is a whole number before converting it to an integer; this stops the crash when a staff member types letters. Finally, a range check confirms that the hire length is from 1 to 8 hours inclusive, which rejects entries such as 0 and 40.

If any check fails, the program displays a message that says what is accepted, such as "Enter a whole number of hours from 1 to 8", and asks again. It doesn't calculate or save the hire until the entry passes all three checks.
mistake: Each check catches a different problem. A blank entry fails the existence check; letters pass it but fail the type check; 40 passes the type check but fails the range check. One check can't stand in for the others.

prompt:
Pobblebonk Escape Rooms in Ballarat takes bookings for groups of 2 to 10 people. Asha wrote the algorithm shown to validate the group size.

Explain the error in Asha's algorithm, give inputs that would show its effect, and state how to correct it.

points.text: Explains that line 3 uses selection (IF), so the check runs only once and the second entry is never checked
Gives inputs that show the effect, e.g. 12 then 15, which produces a booking for 15 guests
Corrects it with a loop, e.g. replacing line 3 with `WHILE guests < 2 OR guests > 10 DO` and line 6 with ENDWHILE, so each new entry is checked until it is valid

model:
Line 3 uses IF, which is selection, so the group size is checked only once. If the first entry is invalid, a second entry is read on line 5, but it is never checked. For example, if the user enters 12 and then 15, the message is displayed once and the algorithm displays "Booked for 15 guests", an invalid booking.

The IF on line 3 should be replaced with a pre-test loop, `WHILE guests < 2 OR guests > 10 DO`, and the ENDIF on line 6 with ENDWHILE, so every new entry is checked until the group size is from 2 to 10.

figures.code:
BEGIN
    INPUT guests
    IF guests < 2 OR guests > 10 THEN
        DISPLAY "Groups of 2 to 10 only"
        INPUT guests
    ENDIF
    DISPLAY "Booked for " + guests + " guests"
END

prompt:
Tilda is building the booking form shown for Bluestone Loop Shuttle, a weekend bus service between Daylesford and nearby wineries. Every booking needs a name and a pick-up stop, and a booking is for 1 to 12 passengers.

Justify the validation, if any, that the program needs for each of the four inputs on the form.

points.text: Name: an existence check, because every booking needs a name and a text box can be left blank
Passengers: a type check before the entry is converted, because the text box accepts any characters, such as "two", which can't be treated as a number (with an existence check that it isn't blank)
Passengers: a range check that the number is from 1 to 12 inclusive, because a booking can't be for 0 or more than 12 passengers
Pick-up stop: only an existence check that a stop has been chosen; the drop-down list offers only valid stops, so type and range checks aren't needed
Return trip: no check is needed, because a check box is always either ticked or not ticked, so it can't hold an invalid value

model:
**Name.** An existence check is needed. Every booking needs a name, and a text box can be left empty, so the program must reject a blank name.

**Passengers.** This is a text box, so the user can type anything. The program needs an existence check, then a type check that the entry is a whole number before it is converted, because an entry such as "two" can't be converted and would otherwise cause an error. It then needs a range check that the number is from 1 to 12 inclusive, because a booking can't be for 0 passengers or for more than the 12 allowed.

**Pick-up stop.** The drop-down list offers only the real stops, so a misspelt or invalid stop can't be entered, and type and range checks aren't needed. The list starts on "Choose a stop", though, so an existence check must confirm that a stop has been chosen.

**Return trip.** No check is needed. A check box is either ticked or not, so it always holds a valid yes or no.
mistake: Justify each input on its own. An existence check on one field doesn't cover the others, a number typed into a text box also needs a type check, and a check box can only be ticked or not, so it needs no check.

prompt:
Mirrim Parking in Traralgon charges $3 for each hour or part of an hour, up to a maximum of $15. Stays of 15 minutes or less are free. During alpha testing, Keira runs the function shown with the test data in the testing table.

Complete the expected output and actual output for tests 2 and 3, and identify the cause of any difference between them.

points.text: Test 2 expected output: $6, because 90 minutes is one hour and part of another
Test 2 actual output: $3
Test 3 expected output and actual output: both $15, because the maximum applies
Identifies the cause: `minutes DIV 60` on line 5 rounds down, so a part hour isn't charged

model:
Test 2: expected output $6, because 90 minutes is one full hour plus part of a second hour. Actual output $3, because line 5 calculates 90 DIV 60 = 1, so only one hour is charged.

Test 3: expected output $15 and actual output $15. 600 minutes is 10 hours, which would cost $30, so the $15 maximum applies, and lines 7 to 9 cap the fee correctly.

The difference in test 2 is caused by line 5: DIV rounds down, so any part hour is ignored. The number of hours should be rounded up instead, for example `hours ← (minutes + 59) DIV 60`.
mistake: Work out the expected output from the charging rules, not by tracing the code. Tracing the code gives the actual output.

figures.code:
FUNCTION parkingFee(minutes)
    IF minutes <= 15 THEN
        fee ← 0
    ELSE
        hours ← minutes DIV 60
        fee ← hours * 3
        IF fee > 15 THEN
            fee ← 15
        ENDIF
    ENDIF
    RETURN fee
ENDFUNCTION

prompt:
Wren is developing a room-booking module for Seagrass Point Community Hall in Port Albert. Rooms can be booked for 1 to 6 hours, and members receive 20% off the hire fee. Before the module is given to hall members for beta testing, Wren will alpha test it.

Describe how Wren should alpha test the module.

points.text: Prepares test data that includes valid, invalid and boundary values, e.g. 1 and 6 hours, 0 and 7 hours and non-numeric entries, for both members and non-members
Records each test in a testing table with columns for the test number, each input (hours and membership), the expected output (worked out from the hall's rules) and the actual output
Where actual output differs from expected output, locates the error with a debugging technique such as a breakpoint or commenting out code, fixes it and re-runs the tests

model: Wren should prepare test data that covers every requirement: a valid length such as 3 hours; the boundary values 1 and 6 hours and the values just outside them, 0 and 7; invalid entries such as text; and bookings by both a member and a non-member, to check the 20% discount. Each test uses a combination of inputs not already tested. She records each test in a testing table, with the test number, a column for each input (hours and membership) and the expected output, calculated by hand from the hall's rules, then runs the module and records the actual output in full. Where the actual output differs from the expected output, she sets a breakpoint, or comments out sections of code, to locate the error, fixes it, and re-runs that test and the earlier tests.
mistake: Each test needs a combination of inputs not already used. Two tests may give the same output, but a repeated combination earns no marks. Write the expected and actual output in full, never shortened.

prompt:
Leilani is alpha testing a pay program for Bellbird Knoll Cherries in Wandin. The module `readPicks` reads each picker's number of buckets from `picks.csv`, `calculatePay` works out each picker's pay at $3.00 a bucket, and `writeSummary` writes the pay summary. For one picker, who picked 160 buckets, the summary shows $48.00 instead of $480.00.

Explain how Leilani could use debugging output statements to find which module contains the error.

points.text: Adds a debugging output statement after `readPicks` that displays the number of buckets read for this picker
Adds a debugging output statement after `calculatePay` that displays the pay it worked out
Works out the correct values by hand to compare with: 160 buckets, and 160 × $3.00 = $480.00

Runs the program and finds the first displayed value that differs from the hand-worked value: wrong buckets point to `readPicks`; correct buckets but wrong pay point to `calculatePay`; both correct point to `writeSummary`

model:
Leilani should add debugging output statements between the modules: one after `readPicks` that displays the number of buckets read for the picker, and one after `calculatePay` that displays the pay it worked out.

Before running the program, she works out the correct values by hand: 160 buckets, and 160 × $3.00 = $480.00. She then runs the program and compares each displayed value with her own. The first value that differs shows where the error is. If the buckets display as 16, `readPicks` is reading the file wrongly; if the buckets are 160 but the pay displays as 48.00, the error is in `calculatePay`; and if the pay displays as 480.00, the error must be in `writeSummary`, for example in how it formats the amount.
mistake: Describing what debugging output is earns little. Explain how the displayed values are compared with values worked out by hand to narrow down where the error is.

prompt:
Hopbush Community Nursing in Maryborough has had a visit-recording app developed for its 30 community nurses, who use it on work tablets to record each home visit, including the client's observations, the care given and any follow-up needed. The app is nearly complete.

Describe how Hopbush Community Nursing should conduct beta testing of the app. Refer to the user group, scenarios, observation and the recording of results.

points.text: User group: how testers are chosen, e.g. a small group of Hopbush nurses selected to represent the range of nurses (experience, age, confidence with technology, kinds of visit), not the developers

Scenarios: realistic tasks stated as goals, e.g. record a visit where a wound dressing was changed and a follow-up visit is needed, carried out on the nurses' work tablets in realistic conditions with test client records
Observation: a developer watches nurses complete the scenarios without helping, noting hesitations, errors and time taken

Documenting results: what is recorded for each nurse and scenario, e.g. a screen recording and the observer's notes on whether it was completed without help, the time taken for each step, where the nurse hesitated or made errors and their comments, used to recommend changes before release

model:
Hopbush Community Nursing should choose about five nurses who reflect the range of its 30 nurses, such as new and experienced nurses, nurses who are more and less confident with technology, and nurses who make different kinds of visits. The developers shouldn't be the testers, because they already know how the app works.

Each nurse should be given realistic scenarios written as goals, such as 'Record a visit where you changed a wound dressing, and book a follow-up visit for next week', and carry them out on their work tablet in realistic conditions, such as in the car between visits, using test client records rather than real ones.

An observer, such as a developer, should watch each nurse work through the scenarios without helping or prompting, so the results show what nurses can do on their own.

The observer should document the results for each nurse and scenario: whether the nurse finished it without help, how long each step took (from a screen recording of the tablet), where they hesitated or made errors, for example while entering the client's observations, and what they said. These results are then used to decide which changes to recommend before the app is released.
mistake: Testers don't check the values the app produces or hunt for bugs; that belongs to alpha testing. Say how the nurses are chosen, what scenario they carry out and what is recorded as they do it, each tied to the nurses' home visits.

prompt:
The developers of Hopbush Community Nursing's visit-recording app have alpha tested every module against a full test table, and every test passed. The nursing manager wants to release the app to all 30 nurses straight away.

Explain why the app should still be beta tested before it is released.

points.text: Alpha testing was done by developers, who know how the app is meant to be used, with planned test data in the development environment
Beta testing puts the app in the hands of actual nurses in realistic conditions, e.g. on their work tablets, in the car between home visits, with little time to spare

So it can find problems alpha testing can't, e.g. nurses who can't find where to record a follow-up visit, or a visit form that takes too long to fill in between appointments, which can then be fixed before all nurses rely on the app

model:
The alpha tests were designed and run by the developers, who already know how the app should be used, with planned test data on development equipment. Passing every test shows that the modules produce the expected outputs, not that nurses can use the app during their rounds.

Beta testing gives the nearly complete app to a group of real nurses, who use it on their work tablets in realistic conditions, such as in the car between home visits with little time to spare. This can uncover problems the developers didn't anticipate, such as nurses who can't find where to record a follow-up visit, or a visit form that takes too long to fill in between appointments. Finding these before release means they can be fixed before all 30 nurses depend on the app.

prompt:
Isla is developing a booking app for Beeac Swim School near Colac. Parents will use it to book and pay for their children's swimming lessons. Eight parents beta tested the app, and Isla recorded the problems shown in the table. She has time to fix only two problems before the app is released next week, and she has chosen problems 1 and 4.

Justify Isla's choice. Refer to the beta test results in your answer.

points.text: Problem 1 stops parents completing the app's main task: payment is refused, so the lesson can't be booked
Problem 4 also stops bookings and is the most widespread serious problem: 5 of 8 testers were affected and 4 of them gave up before choosing a lesson
The other problems didn't stop anyone booking: problems 2 and 3 are only cosmetic, and in problem 5 the booking had still been made

Links the choice to the release: fixing the problems that stop bookings protects the swim school's bookings and income and parents' trust at launch, while the minor problems can wait for a later update

model:
Problem 1 stops parents doing the one thing the app exists for. When a card number is typed with spaces, payment is refused and the lesson isn't booked. Three of the eight testers met it, so many parents would meet it after release.

Problem 4 is the most widespread serious problem. Five of the eight testers had to wait about 20 seconds for the timetable, and four of them gave up before they had even chosen a lesson, so it also stops bookings.

The other problems don't stop anyone booking. Problems 2 and 3 were only noticed, and in problem 5 the booking had been made, even though the late email left parents unsure. With time for only two fixes, fixing the problems that stop parents booking protects the swim school's bookings and parents' trust when the app is released, and the minor problems can be fixed in a later update.
mistake: Counting affected testers isn't enough on its own. Problem 2 affected all eight testers but stopped no one booking. Weigh how serious each problem is as well as how many testers met it.

figures.title: Problems found in beta testing (8 testers)
rows: Payment is refused when the card number is typed with spaces
Could not finish booking a lesson
The Confirm button is a different blue from the school's logo
A spelling error on the Help screen ('lesons')
The lesson timetable takes about 20 seconds to load on older phones
Four gave up before choosing a lesson
The booking confirmation email arrives up to an hour late
Booking was made, but they were unsure it had worked

prompt:
Tarrone Community Health in Warrnambool will launch a new check-in kiosk program at the start of February. The software requirements specification states that clients must be able to check in within one minute, and that clients with low vision must be able to check in without help.

Describe an evaluation strategy for the kiosk program. Refer to two evaluation criteria and the data to be collected for each, the time frame, and who is responsible.

points.text: A measurable efficiency criterion based on the one-minute requirement, e.g. at least 90% of check-ins are completed in under one minute
A measurable effectiveness (accessibility) criterion based on the low-vision requirement, e.g. at least 9 of 10 low-vision clients observed check in without staff help
Suitable data and method for each criterion, e.g. the kiosk's log of start and finish times for every check-in; observation of low-vision clients, with a record of whether each needed help
Time frame: after the kiosk has been in normal use for several weeks (e.g. data collected in March and April, reported in May), so clients are past the learning stage

Responsibility: who collects or provides the data and who reports, e.g. the IT officer exports the kiosk log, reception staff record the observations, and the practice manager compares the results with the criteria

model:
Criterion 1 (efficiency): at least 90% of check-ins are completed in under one minute. The kiosk program would log the start and finish time of every check-in, so the percentage completed within one minute can be calculated.

Criterion 2 (effectiveness, accessibility): at least 9 of 10 clients with low vision can check in without help from staff. Reception staff would observe a sample of low-vision clients as they check in and record whether each one needed help.

Time frame: data would be collected from the start of March, once clients have had several weeks to get used to the kiosk, until the end of April, and the results would be reported in May.

Responsibility: the clinic's IT officer would export the kiosk's check-in log at the end of each month, the reception staff would record the observations, and the practice manager would compare the results with both criteria and write the report.

prompt:
Tarrone Community Health's manager wants to evaluate the new check-in kiosk program in its first week of use, 'while it is still fresh'. One evaluation criterion is that at least 90% of check-ins are completed in under one minute.

Explain why the evaluation should take place later.

points.text: In the first week most clients are using the kiosk for the first time and are still learning, so check-ins are slower and more help is needed than in normal use
So data from that week reflects the learning stage, not everyday use, and judging it against the one-minute criterion would give a misleading result

model: In the first week, most clients will be using the kiosk for the first time, so they will be slower and more likely to ask staff for help than once they are familiar with it. Check-in times from that week would reflect the learning stage rather than normal use, so comparing them with the one-minute criterion would make the kiosk seem less efficient than it really is. Waiting several weeks gives data about everyday use.

prompt:
Iraak Table Grapes near Mildura is introducing a program that tracks each pallet of grapes from the packing shed to the truck. The program goes live in early October. Most of the year's packing happens in the harvest, from December to April. In October and November only a few permanent staff work in the shed, and extra packers are employed for the harvest from early December.

The manager, Declan, plans to collect the evaluation data in November. The developer, Ngoc, suggests collecting it in January and February instead.

Justify Ngoc's suggestion.

points.text: In November only a few staff are working and few pallets are packed, so data from then wouldn't reflect how the program is normally used
January and February fall in the harvest, when the whole packing team uses the program at full volume, so the data shows how well it performs under its real workload
The extra packers start in early December, so by January they have had several weeks to learn the program, and the data reflects everyday use rather than the learning stage

model:
Collecting the data in November would give a misleading picture. Only a few permanent staff are in the shed then and few pallets are packed, so the data wouldn't show how the program performs in the season it was built for.

January and February are in the middle of the harvest, when the whole packing team is tracking pallets at full volume. Data from then shows whether the program meets its criteria under its real workload, such as when many pallets are being loaded onto trucks at once.

The extra packers start in early December. By January they have used the program for several weeks, so their data reflects everyday use, not the slower work of people still learning a new program.
mistake: A justification must use the scenario. 'It is better to wait' earns little. Say why November's data would mislead here (few staff, few pallets) and why January and February suit (the full harvest workload, and packers who are past the learning stage).

prompt:
High Plains Outdoors in Mansfield has launched a new online store. Two of its evaluation criteria are:

1. Customers can complete a purchase in under three minutes.
2. At least 80% of customers are satisfied with the checkout process.

For each criterion, identify a suitable data collection technique and justify your choice.

points.text: Criterion 1: analyse the store's system logs of the time between starting checkout and the order being confirmed (or time a sample of customers while observing them)
Justification for criterion 1: gives measured times, which can be checked directly against the three-minute target, rather than customers' estimates
Criterion 2: an online survey or questionnaire with a satisfaction rating, sent to customers after they buy
Justification for criterion 2: satisfaction is an opinion only customers can give; a survey reaches many customers quickly and the ratings can be totalled as a percentage to compare with 80%

model:
Criterion 1: I would analyse the online store's system logs, which record when each customer starts checkout and when the order is confirmed. This gives an accurate, measured time for every purchase without disturbing customers, and the times can be checked directly against the three-minute target.

Criterion 2: I would email a short online survey to customers after each purchase, asking them to rate their satisfaction with checkout from 1 to 5. Satisfaction is an opinion that only customers can report, and a survey reaches many of them quickly. The number of satisfied customers can be converted to a percentage and compared with the 80% target.
mistake: Using a survey to measure time is a common error. Time-based criteria need measured times, from system logs or by timing users.

prompt:
Mooralla Shire Council has built an online permit system so that residents can apply for building permits without phoning or visiting the council office. To evaluate the criterion 'Residents can lodge an application without needing help from council staff', the project manager plans to survey the 12 council staff who process applications.

Explain one weakness of this plan and recommend a better data collection technique.

points.text: Weakness: council staff are not the people the criterion is about; residents lodge the applications
So staff can only guess or pass on second-hand reports of whether residents needed help, and their answers won't reliably show whether the criterion is met

Better technique that collects data from or about residents, e.g. a short survey shown to residents as they lodge an application, asking whether they needed help; or counting permit help calls in the council's call records against the number of applications

model:
The criterion is about residents, but the plan collects data only from council staff, who process applications rather than lodge them. Staff can only guess, or pass on what a few residents have told them, about whether residents needed help, so the data won't reliably show whether the criterion has been met.

A better technique is a short online survey shown to residents as soon as they lodge an application, asking whether they needed help from council staff to complete it. This collects data directly from the people the criterion is about, and the responses can be totalled.

prompt:
Streatham Rural Supplies in Skipton launched an online ordering program in March. Two of its evaluation criteria are:

1. At least 90% of online orders are dispatched within 24 hours of being placed.
2. The average time for staff to process a return is under 4 minutes.

The program's logs for May and June show that 444 of the 480 online orders were dispatched within 24 hours. In June, staff timed 8 returns, as shown in the table.

Explain whether each criterion has been met. Use the data in your answer.

points.text: Criterion 1: 444 ÷ 480 = 92.5% of orders were dispatched within 24 hours
92.5% is at least the 90% target, so criterion 1 is met
Criterion 2: the 8 times total 34.4 minutes, so the average is 34.4 ÷ 8 = 4.3 minutes
4.3 minutes is not under the 4-minute target, so criterion 2 is not met

model:
Criterion 1 is met. In May and June, 444 of the 480 online orders were dispatched within 24 hours, which is 444 ÷ 480 = 92.5%. That is above the target of at least 90%.

Criterion 2 is not met. The eight return times total 34.4 minutes, so the average is 34.4 ÷ 8 = 4.3 minutes. The target was an average under 4 minutes, and 4.3 minutes is above it, even though three of the returns took less than 4 minutes.
mistake: State the figure and the target side by side ('92.5% against a target of 90%: met'). A judgement such as 'most orders went out quickly' gives no evidence and earns little.

prompt:
Tyntynder Coachlines in Swan Hill has replaced phone bookings with an online booking program for its coach services. The table shows three of the program's evaluation criteria and the data collected in weeks 5 to 12 after launch.

Evaluate the efficiency and effectiveness of the booking program. Use the data in your answer.

points.text: Criterion 1: an average booking time of 2 minutes 10 seconds is under the 3-minute target, so it is met
Criterion 2: 14 passengers with an online booking were missing from the passenger list, but every booking must appear, so it is not met
Criterion 3: 172 ÷ 200 = 86% rated the program 4 or 5, which reaches the target of at least 80%, so it is met
Efficiency: criterion 1 measures the time and effort customers spend booking, so meeting it shows the program is efficient

Effectiveness: criteria 2 and 3 measure how well the program achieves its purpose; it is easy to use (usability) but its passenger lists are incomplete (completeness), so it is only partly effective, e.g. drivers may not expect passengers who have booked

model:
Criterion 1 is met. The average booking time was 2 minutes 10 seconds, which is under the 3-minute target. Criterion 2 is not met. Drivers found 14 passengers holding an online booking who weren't on the passenger list, and the criterion requires every booking to appear. Criterion 3 is met. 172 of the 200 customers surveyed (86%) rated the program 4 or 5 for ease of use, above the 80% target.

Criterion 1 measures the time and effort customers spend making a booking, so meeting it shows that the program is efficient.

Criteria 2 and 3 measure how well the program achieves its purpose, so they show its effectiveness. It does well on usability, because customers find it easy to use, but it falls short on completeness, because its passenger lists leave out some bookings, so drivers may not be expecting passengers who have booked. The program is therefore only partly effective. Overall it is efficient, but it won't be fully effective until the fault that leaves bookings off the passenger lists is fixed.
mistake: Stopping at 'met' or 'not met' leaves the evaluation unfinished: say what the results show. Time, cost and effort are measures of efficiency; how well the program achieves its purpose (such as accuracy, completeness and usability) is effectiveness. A program can be quick to use and still not be fully effective.

figures.title: Tyntynder Coachlines booking program: evaluation data, weeks 5 to 12
rows: 1. The average time for a customer to complete a booking is under 3 minutes.
System log of 1 240 bookings: average time 2 minutes 10 seconds
2. Every booking appears on the driver's passenger list for that trip.
Drivers' records: 14 passengers showed an online booking but were not on the passenger list
3. At least 80% of surveyed customers rate the program 4 or 5 out of 5 for ease of use.
Survey of 200 customers chosen at random: 172 gave a rating of 4 or 5

prompt:
Jarrah Lane Software is building a membership program for the Narrawong Sailing Club. During coding, the club president asks for an event-booking feature that isn't in the software requirements specification, and the developers agree to add it without changing the plan. In the same week, the team's lead developer is moved to another project.

Explain how each of these two factors could affect the effectiveness of the project plan.

points.text: Identifies the event-booking request as scope creep: new work added after the scope was agreed, without the plan being changed

Effect of the scope creep: the Gantt chart has no time for designing, coding and testing the feature, so coding runs over, later tasks and milestones slip, testing time is squeezed, or effort is drawn away from the agreed requirements so they may not all be met
Identifies the lead developer's move as a change in personnel: their tasks must be reassigned
Effect of the personnel change: other developers need time to learn the lead developer's code, so those tasks take longer and, if they are on the critical path, the handover date moves

model:
The event-booking feature is scope creep, because it adds work after the scope was agreed in the SRS and the plan hasn't been changed to allow for it. The Gantt chart has no time for designing, coding and testing the feature, so coding will run over, the tasks that depend on it will start late, and testing time may be cut to hold the deadline, which risks releasing a program with more errors. The time spent on the extra feature is also taken from the membership features the club asked for, which may not all be finished.

The lead developer's move is a change in personnel. Their unfinished tasks must be given to other developers, who need time to understand code they didn't write. Those tasks will take longer than estimated, and if they are on the critical path, the program will be handed over to the club later than planned.
mistake: Scope creep doesn't give the client a better product. Unplanned extras draw time and effort away from the agreed requirements, which may not all be met.

prompt:
Dooen Meter Services in Horsham is having a meter-reading app developed. The Gantt chart shows the plan, in days. The laptop used to build the database fails, and Code database takes 5 days longer than planned.

Explain the effect of this delay on the release date. Use the Gantt chart in your answer.

points.text: Code database is not on the critical path (Analyse needs → Design app screens → Code app screens → Connect app to database → Alpha test → Beta test), which plans the release for day 28
Code database was due to finish on day 13, while Connect app to database can't start until Code app screens finishes on day 16; with the 5-day delay it finishes on day 18
So Connect app to database starts 2 days late and the release moves from day 28 to day 30, 2 days late; the database tasks are now on the critical path

model:
The critical path is Analyse needs, Design app screens, Code app screens, Connect app to database, Alpha test and Beta test, which plans the release for day 28. Code database isn't on this path: it was due to finish on day 13, while Connect app to database can't start until Code app screens finishes on day 16.

With the 5-day delay, Code database finishes on day 18. Connect app to database has to wait for it, so it starts 2 days late, and every later task moves by 2 days. The release moves from day 28 to day 30. The path through Design database and Code database is now the critical path.
mistake: Don't assume the whole 5-day delay passes to the release date. A task off the critical path moves the finish only by the amount its delay exceeds the time its path had to spare.

figures.title: Dooen Meter Services meter-reading app
figures.caption: Connect app to database starts when both coding tasks have finished.

prompt:
Hazel is developing a membership program for the Ballangeich Junior Football League near Warrnambool. Halfway through coding, the league asks for two extra features.

- **Request A:** an SMS reminder before each training night. Hazel estimates it will take 4 days. The league agrees to move the handover 4 days later, and Hazel adds the task to her plan.
- **Request B:** a page showing each player's goal tally. Hazel thinks it will take only a day, so she adds it without changing her plan. It takes 3 days.

Explain which request is an example of scope creep, and how each request affects the effectiveness of Hazel's project plan.

points.text: Identifies request B as scope creep: work added after the scope was agreed on a quick guess, with no change to the plan or the handover date agreed with the league

Explains that request A is a controlled change: it was estimated and agreed, and the task and the new handover date were added to the plan, so the plan still matches the work and remains a reliable guide

Explains the effect of request B: the plan has no time for its 3 days of work, so coding and the tasks after it slip, the handover is late or testing is squeezed to hold the date, and the plan no longer reflects what is really happening

model:
Request B is scope creep. The goal tally page was added after the scope had been agreed, on a quick guess of its size, with no change to the plan or the handover date agreed with the league.

Request A also adds work, but it is a controlled change. Hazel estimated it, the league agreed to a handover 4 days later, and the task was added to the plan. The plan still matches the work being done, so it remains a reliable guide to when the program will be ready.

Request B makes the plan less effective. Its 3 days of work aren't in the plan, so coding finishes later than planned and the tasks that depend on it slip. Either the handover is late, or Hazel squeezes testing to hold the date, which risks releasing a program with more errors. Either way, the plan no longer shows what is really happening.
mistake: A request isn't scope creep just because it arrives late. It becomes scope creep when the work is added without being properly assessed and agreed, and without changing the plan.

prompt:
Gherang Gap Software in Geelong is building a court-booking and membership program for the Moorabool Flats Croquet Club. The task *Code booking module*, which is on the critical path, is running a week behind. To catch up, the project manager, Teodora, plans to move Bashir, a developer who has been working on another client's project, onto the task for its last two weeks.

Explain why this change could reduce the effectiveness of Gherang Gap Software's project plans.

points.text: Bashir is new to the project, so he needs time to learn its requirements, design and existing code before he can contribute (and may make errors that need fixing), so the task won't speed up as much as Teodora expects
The developers already on the task must spend time explaining the code to him and checking his work, which takes time away from their own coding, so the task can fall further behind

Code booking module is on the critical path, so if the move slows the task further instead of recovering the week, the delay passes to the tasks that depend on it and to the handover, and the plan has to be revised again, making it a less reliable guide
Alternative: moving Bashir leaves the other client's project a developer short, so its tasks slip and its plan has to be changed too

model:
Bashir hasn't worked on the croquet club's program, so before he can help he needs time to learn its requirements, its design and the code already written, and while he is learning he may make mistakes that need fixing. His first days add little, so the task won't catch up as quickly as Teodora expects.

The developers already on the task also have to stop and explain the code to him and check his work. That time comes out of their own coding, so the task can fall even further behind.

Code booking module is on the critical path. If the move slows the task further instead of recovering the week, the tasks that depend on it and the handover are delayed. Teodora would then have to revise the plan again, so it becomes a less reliable guide to when the program will be finished.
mistake: Moving a developer across is itself a personnel change, one of the three factors. Adding a person to a late task doesn't recover time straight away: Bashir must first learn the project, and the developers already on it give up coding time to help him.

prompt:
Nadia is the only developer building a volunteer rostering program for the Dunmore Creek Netball Association. Her project plan is a Gantt chart, and the program must be ready before the season starts.

Describe two techniques Nadia could use to record the progress of her project, and how each would help her.

points.text: Technique 1: a dated development journal or log recording tasks worked on, time spent, problems met, and decisions with reasons
How it helps: explains the causes of delays and why changes were made, giving evidence for assessing the plan, and helps her pick up work after a break
Technique 2: annotating the Gantt chart (or using project management software) with actual start and finish dates, percentage complete and reasons for changes, while keeping the planned dates
How it helps: shows planned against actual progress at a glance, so she can see early whether a delay threatens the start of the season and adjust dependent tasks
Alternative technique: adjusting the plan's time frames and tasks as work runs late or early (for example, extending a task and moving the tasks that depend on it), while keeping the original dates
How it helps: the plan stays realistic, so she can see whether the program will still be ready for the season and which later tasks need to change

model:
Nadia could keep a development journal, writing a dated entry each session that records the tasks she worked on, how long they took, any problems and how she solved them, and decisions with her reasons. Because she works alone, this explains later why tasks took longer than planned, and it gives her evidence when she assesses her project plan.

She could also annotate her Gantt chart as she goes, adding actual start and finish dates, the percentage of each task complete and short notes giving the reason for each change and its effect on later tasks, while keeping the original dates visible. This lets her compare planned and actual progress at a glance and see early whether a delay will push the program past the start of the season, so she can adjust later tasks in time.
mistake: Describing what a Gantt chart looks like earns nothing here. Say how Nadia would update it and compare actual with planned progress to see whether she is ahead or behind.

prompt:
Nadia's coding took a week longer than planned, so she moved her testing tasks a week later on her Gantt chart, writing over the original dates.

Explain why she should have kept the original dates.

points.text: Keeping the original dates beside the adjusted or actual dates lets planned and actual progress be compared
That comparison is the evidence needed to assess the effectiveness of her project plan, e.g. it shows her coding estimate was a week short, so future plans can be more realistic
Alternative for the second mark: the original dates record that a change was made, so the number of changes to the plan and their impact on completion can be reviewed when the plan is assessed

model: By writing over the original dates, Nadia has lost the record of what she planned. If she had kept them beside the adjusted dates, she could compare planned and actual progress. That comparison is the evidence she needs when assessing her project plan: it would show that her coding estimate was a week short, which she could allow for in future plans.

prompt:
Kanawinka Software in Hamilton has four developers building a stock program for a farm machinery dealer. Two work in the Hamilton office, and two work from home in Portland and Casterton. The project plan has more than 40 tasks, and many of them depend on each other. At present the project manager keeps the Gantt chart on a whiteboard in the Hamilton office and updates it by hand each Friday.

Recommend a better way for the team to record its progress, and justify your recommendation.

points.text: Recommends shared online project management software that each developer updates as their tasks progress

Justification tied to the team's locations: the developers in Portland and Casterton can't see the whiteboard, but everyone can see and update the same current plan, at any time rather than only on Fridays

Justification tied to the dependencies: with more than 40 linked tasks, entering a task's actual dates makes the software move the tasks that depend on it and show whether the critical path and finish date have changed, which is slow and error-prone to do by hand
Alternative justification: the software keeps planned and actual dates side by side, giving evidence for assessing the plan at the end of the project

model:
I recommend that the team use shared online project management software, with each developer entering the actual progress of their own tasks as they go.

Two of the four developers work from Portland and Casterton, so they can't see a whiteboard in the Hamilton office. With shared software, everyone works from the same current plan at any time, not only after the Friday update.

The plan has more than 40 tasks that depend on each other. When a developer enters that a task has finished late, the software moves every task that depends on it and shows whether the critical path and the finish date have changed. Redrawing a whiteboard chart by hand is slow, and dependent tasks are easily missed.
mistake: Naming the software isn't enough for a recommendation. The marks are for the reasons, and they must fit this team: developers in three towns and more than 40 dependent tasks.

prompt:
Josie and Anil are developing an orders and stock program for Bena Hills Olive Oil in Korumburra. Their project plan is a Gantt chart. The table shows an excerpt from their project log.

Describe one problem caused by how these entries record changes to the plan. Then recommend two different improvements to the way Josie and Anil record their progress.

points.text: Problem: the entries say only that a task is late, on schedule or early, with no reason for the change and no effect on later tasks or the completion date, so the team can't judge how each change affects the plan, either while the project runs or when the plan is assessed (e.g. whether the order screen's four-day delay moved the handover)
Recommendation: record the reason each change was necessary, e.g. what caused the order screen to fall four days behind
Recommendation: record the impact of each change on the tasks that depend on it, the critical path and the completion date
Alternative recommendation: record the adjustment made in response, i.e. which tasks or time frames were changed and to what, beside the original dates
Alternative recommendation: annotate each change on the Gantt chart and keep a count of the changes, so the number of changes made to the plan can be reviewed when the plan is assessed

model:
**Problem:** The entries record only that a task was late, on schedule or early. They don't say why the order screen fell four days behind, or whether that delay (or the stock report finishing early) moved the tasks that depend on it and the handover date. Josie and Anil therefore can't tell how each change affects the rest of the plan while the work goes on, and when the plan is assessed they won't be able to explain the delay.

**Recommendation 1:** For every change, record the reason it was necessary, such as the cause of the order screen's four-day delay.

**Recommendation 2:** For every change, record its impact on the tasks that depend on it, the critical path and the completion date, for example whether the order screen's delay pushes back testing and the handover.
mistake: Recommendations that fix the project itself, such as adding a developer to the order screen or estimating coding better, earn nothing: the question asks how progress is recorded. Two wordings of one idea, such as 'give reasons' and 'explain why it happened', score only once.

prompt:
Thomson River Dental in Sale had a booking program developed. The tasks ran one after another. The table shows the planned and actual durations, with notes from the developer's journal.

Evaluate the effectiveness of the project plan. Refer to the data in your answer.

points.text: Overall result from the data: 32 days against 29 planned, so the handover was 3 days late

A strength supported by the data: three of the five estimates (Interview staff, Design screens, Code reports) were exactly right; or adding a second tester cut Test from 5 days to 3, recovering 2 of the 5 days lost
Weakness: Code booking module ran 5 days over because SMS reminders, not in the SRS, were added without changing the plan (scope creep), so the plan had no control over changes
Judgement weighing the evidence: the plan was only partly effective, because its estimates were sound and it was adjusted to recover time, but uncontrolled scope creep still made the handover late

model:
The project took 32 days against the 29 planned, so the booking program was handed over 3 days late.

The plan's time estimates were mostly realistic: Interview staff, Design screens and Code reports each took exactly as long as planned. The plan was also adjusted well once it slipped: adding a second tester cut Test from 5 days to 3, recovering 2 of the days lost.

Its main weakness was that it had no way of controlling changes. Code booking module took 15 days instead of 10 because the practice manager's request for SMS reminders, which wasn't in the SRS, was added without changing the plan. This is scope creep.

Overall the plan was only partly effective. Its estimates were sound and it was adjusted to recover time, but uncontrolled scope creep still made the handover 3 days late. Future plans should put new requests through a change process that adjusts the schedule before work begins.
mistake: A judgement needs evidence. Quote the planned and actual figures and give the cause of each difference, rather than just saying the project was late.

prompt:
Thomson River Dental's booking program was handed over 3 days late, after SMS reminders were added part-way through coding without the plan being changed. Two months later, the practice manager said: 'Patients love the new program, so the project plan must have been effective.'

Explain why this reasoning is flawed.

points.text: Patients' satisfaction is evidence about the solution (part of evaluating its effectiveness), not about the project plan

The plan is judged by comparing planned and actual progress; here it finished 3 days late because of uncontrolled scope change, so the plan was only partly effective even though the program is popular

model: Patients' views are evidence about the solution: they help evaluate how effective the booking program is. The project plan is judged separately, by comparing what was planned with what actually happened. Here the project finished 3 days late because SMS reminders were added without changing the plan, so the plan was only partly effective, even though the program itself is popular.

prompt:
Imogen managed the development of a loans and bookings program for Marnoo Community Library near St Arnaud. The program had to be running by 1 February, when the licence for the library's old system ran out. The tasks ran one after another. The table shows the planned and actual durations, with notes from Imogen's journal. The program went live 5 days late.

Recommend two improvements to Imogen's next project plan. Justify each recommendation using the evidence in the table.

points.text: Recommendation 1: plan time to fix the problems found in beta testing and retest, for example as a separate task after beta testing
Justification 1: beta testing took 6 days instead of 3 because the 11 problems found had to be fixed and retested with no time planned for it, which caused 3 of the 5 days' delay

Recommendation 2: build some spare time into the plan before a date that can't move, for example by planning to finish several days before the old licence runs out (or: arrange a backup place to run and test the code if the server fails)

Justification 2: the 2-day server outage during coding couldn't have been predicted; with a few spare days before 1 February, a delay like this would have been absorbed instead of pushing go-live past the date (or a backup would have let coding and testing continue)

model:
First, Imogen should plan time to fix the problems that beta testing finds and to retest the fixes, for example as a separate task after beta testing. Her plan allowed 3 days for beta testing, but it took 6, because the testers found 11 problems and no time had been planned to fix them. That accounts for 3 of the 5 days the program was late.

Second, she should build some spare time into the plan before a date that can't move, by planning to finish a few days before the old system's licence runs out. The test server was down for 2 days during coding, which no one could have predicted. With a few spare days before 1 February, that delay would have been absorbed instead of pushing go-live past the date the old system stopped.
mistake: 'Make better estimates' is too vague, and two versions of one idea earn only one mark. Give two different changes to the plan, each backed by the figures in the table.
